GCTS research notebook · 6 November 2026 UTC

Reusable Wang fragments and learned tactic selection

On 16 first-order inputs, lifted search found 11 proofs. Adding a bounded ground-unit pass raised that to 14. The learned selector and three fixed hybrid schedules found the same 14. Each reported proof was checked from the original statement through the same translation-only Wang palette.

A frozen bank also reused checked tile fragments across changes in symbol names. The right-associated 23-choice proof reused all 207 fragments from the bank. The balanced version needed two fresh fragments after donor and within-proof reuse.

DiscoveryGrounding exclusionsTile reuseTile viewerProof linesReplay

Choose how to search before checking the tiles

The unit tactic grounds only terms up to a fixed depth. It propagates known unit clauses through their complementary literals, recording one resolution for each deletion. A contradiction gives a dependency graph of source instances and resolutions. The fallback runs the existing lifted prover, which can unify variables directly and derive clauses beyond unit propagation.

The selector groups formulas by observable features such as term nesting, biconditionals, and existential quantifiers. During 180 development episodes it tried one schedule at a time, explored randomly, and used the average observed loss in each group. It froze before the 16-input evaluation. The feature design followed preliminary experiments. The evaluated inputs stayed out of the policy’s reward updates.

The learned selector used 280,982 work units on the 14 solved cases. The fixed depth-zero pass followed by lifted search used 274,397. These are deterministic work proxies. For grounding they count terms, schema checks, enumerated assignments, and visits to clauses that watch a complementary literal. For lifted search they count input clauses, proposals, and unification equations. The comparison is within this implementation.

The family exercise reached the search limit. A finite countermodel independently refutes the quantifier-swap control. The capital and family inputs come from the tutorial. TPTP first-order tutorial

Exclude substitutions by their term-tree addresses

A variable below \(d\) function symbols can receive a term of depth at most \(D-d\) when the ground instance has depth limit \(D\). Record its deepest occurrence. A constant already deeper than \(D\) excludes the entire clause. The checker reads the certified address and independently checks every other occurrence before allowing the restriction.

For \(P(x,f(x))\), the marked occurrence of \(x\) is the child of \(f\) in the second argument. With \(D=1\), that occurrence admits a constant and excludes a term of depth one.

The recorded address is [0,1,0] in zero-based literal, argument, and child order. The forged address [0,0] points to the first argument.

At the Peano addition depth-one trial, the address bounds reduced the set of candidate assignments from 112,505 to 6,622 before the instance limit stopped enumeration. The exact grounding control compared 101 bounded cases with literal Cartesian enumeration and rejected a certificate that used a shallower occurrence of a repeated variable.

Reuse a checked patch under a reversible name map

A fragment takes a source schema or earlier ground clauses and returns one clause. Rename its symbol codes in first-occurrence order throughout its complete input and output. This preserves which symbols are equal, where they occur, and how the tile computation uses them. The checker requires an injective receiver map and compares the full reconstructed boundary text. It then checks sorts and links the decoded clauses to the exact earlier lines.

Across the earlier nine proofs, the 333 exact fragment strings reduce to 108 canonical shapes. In the new experiment the donor bank is frozen at six earlier proofs. Each proof can also reuse a fragment checked earlier within that proof. The Peano successor example is a same-proof cache control. The addition and incidence examples test other proofs.
